drapeaux.note: English wording copied from the passage of Manetti quoted on webexhibits.org (White's 1968 translation); two phrases are shortened with quotation marks kept on verbatim fragments only.

accroche: Around 1415, a Florentine architect drills a hole in a painting and holds up a mirror. What he lets us see exists in no painting before him.
contenu_vulgarise:
In the early 15th century, the Florentine architect Filippo Brunelleschi paints a small panel showing the Baptistery of Florence, seen from inside the neighboring cathedral, then still unfinished. Nothing in the subject sets this picture apart from any other city view. The apparatus Brunelleschi builds around it, however, has no known equivalent before that date.

The most detailed account of the experiment comes from a biography of Brunelleschi written in the 1480s by Antonio di Tuccio Manetti, who claims to have had the panel in his hands and to have seen it several times.

## Looking Through a Hole to See a Mirror

The panel is pierced by a hole, placed at the point from which the scene is viewed. According to Manetti, it is as small as a lentil on the painted side, and on the back it widens into a cone, like a woman's straw hat, to the size of a ducat or a little more. The viewer puts his eye to the back, where the hole is large, and holds a mirror in the other hand, facing the painting. What he sees is the reflection of the painting, not the painting itself. Where the sky should be, Brunelleschi placed burnished silver, which reflects the real air and in which the clouds are carried along by the wind: the boundary between the painted image and the real scene blurs.

The effect, according to Manetti, was striking: one believed one was seeing the real thing. What Brunelleschi works out with this apparatus is a way of representing, accurately, on a flat surface, a scene viewed from a fixed point. Manetti and Vasari concluded that he had invented perspective.

The exact date of the experiment remains debated among art historians: according to Manetti, his experiments fall between 1415 and 1420, while others propose a date before 1413 (Kemp), 1401 to 1409 (Gioseffi), or 1425 (Edgerton). The original panel has not survived: both panels Brunelleschi painted are lost.

## From a Private Experiment to a Public Rule

Brunelleschi publishes nothing: his demonstration remains an apparatus to be shown, not a treatise to be read. It is the humanist Leon Battista Alberti who writes, in 1435, his treatise on painting, *De pictura*, the first description of geometric linear perspective. Alberti credits the discovery to Brunelleschi and dedicates the treatise to him: the dedication openly acknowledges a debt.

What tradition keeps from the experiment is not only how paintings look: a mirror held up before a hole, one day in early 15th-century Florence, became, in Manetti's account, the birth of a way of painting that calculates the place of everything from a single point of view.

repere.texte: According to Manetti, the hole is "as small as a lentil" on the painted side and widens on the back "like a woman's straw hat" to the size of a ducat or a little more; the eye is placed on the back, where the hole is large. Manetti adds: "I have had the painting in my hand and have seen it many times in these days, so I can give testimony." The original panel has not survived.
repere.source: Antonio di Tuccio Manetti, Life of Brunelleschi (1480s), White's 1968 English translation as quoted by webexhibits.org

carte.punch: A hole in a painting, a mirror held up in front: that is how Western perspective is born.
carte.idee: Around 1415, according to Manetti, Brunelleschi paints the Florence Baptistery on a panel pierced with a hole, to be viewed by reflection in a mirror. The experiment shows that a scene viewed from a fixed point can be transferred accurately onto a flat surface.

quiz.question: What exactly does Brunelleschi's panel-and-mirror experiment demonstrate?
choix: That oil paint, still rare in Florence at that date, renders light far better than the tempera used until then
That the Florence Baptistery had been poorly proportioned by the Romanesque architects who built it three centuries earlier
That a polished, well-oriented mirror can replace a painted panel in the interior decoration of a religious building
That a scene viewed from a fixed point can be accurately transferred onto a flat surface
quiz.explication: Brunelleschi's apparatus shows that a scene viewed from a fixed point can be reproduced accurately on a flat surface: the viewer compares the reflection of the painting with the real scene. It is neither a comparison of painting techniques, nor a judgment on the Baptistery, nor a decorative use of the mirror, which serves here only as a verification tool.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does the viewer look at Brunelleschi's painted panel, according to the procedure described by Manetti?
choix: He puts his eye to the back of the panel, against the hole, and holds a mirror up facing the painting with his other hand
He observes the panel from a distance, without any special device, from the Baptistery's forecourt
He looks at the panel through a magnifying lens fixed on a stand
He observes only the panel's reflection in the water of a basin
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Manetti describes the procedure precisely: the viewer puts his eye to the back, where the hole is large, and holds a mirror up facing the painting with his other hand. What he sees then is the reflection of the painting in the mirror, not the painting itself.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What covers the sky portion of the panel, and what effect does it produce?
choix: A thin sheet of polished silver, which reflects the real sky and its moving clouds
A layer of dark blue paint, to heighten the contrast with the rest of the panel
A plate of tinted glass, which gives an effect of artificial depth
Nothing in particular: the sky is painted like the rest of the picture
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to Manetti, Brunelleschi placed burnished silver where the sky should be, so that the real air is reflected in it and the clouds in it are carried along by the wind: the boundary between the painted image and the real scene blurs.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who writes, in 1435, the treatise that first describes geometric linear perspective?
choix: Leon Battista Alberti, in De pictura
Filippo Brunelleschi himself, in a treatise that remained in manuscript
Antonio di Tuccio Manetti, in his biography of the 1480s
Andreas Werckmeister, in an architecture treatise
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Brunelleschi publishes nothing; his demonstration remains an apparatus to be shown. It is Leon Battista Alberti who writes the treatise De pictura in 1435, the first description of geometric linear perspective, and who credits the discovery to Brunelleschi.
